pieces.title: The experiment worked, but her name was not on the Nobel list: Chien-Shiung Wu
pieces.hook: Design the decisive question as an experiment no one can work around: theories can be debated; instrument readings end the argument.
pieces.takeaway: Design the decisive question as an experiment no one can work around: theories can be debated; instrument readings end the argument.
pieces.imageCredit: Science Service (Smithsonian Institution collection) · no known copyright restrictions (Smithsonian Flickr Commons), Wikimedia Commons

parts: Chien-Shiung Wu (1912–1997) was born in Liuhe, Taicang, Jiangsu. A nuclear physicist, she later became a U.S. citizen. In the laboratory she overturned a symmetry that had seemed only natural — and then did not share the Nobel Prize stage with the theorists who had proposed the idea.

paras.lead: Her father opened the schoolhouse door to girls
parts: She was born in Taicang on 31 May 1912. Her father, Wu Zhongyi, founded Mingde School and admitted girls. She began her education there, later attended Suzhou Women’s Normal School and National Central University, and graduated from the physics department in 1934.

In 1936 she went to the United States to study at the University of California, Berkeley, and received her doctorate in 1940. Her research brought her into nuclear physics and radioactivity; the circle of her advisers was closely tied to Ernest Lawrence’s Radiation Laboratory.

She later married the physicist Luke Chia-Liu Yuan. During the Second World War she worked at Columbia University on projects related to the Manhattan Project, improving radiation detection and providing experimental support for the gaseous-diffusion method of isotope separation. After the war she became one of the most relied-upon experimentalists in the field of beta decay.

In the spring of 1956, Tsung-Dao Lee discussed a question with her: in the weak interaction, did left–right symmetry — parity — have to hold? Chen-Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee then wrote a paper questioning the law, published in October. Wu judged that a beta-decay experiment with cobalt-60 polarized at extremely low temperature was a “golden opportunity” to test it, and must not be missed.

She sought a collaboration with the low-temperature group at the U.S. National Bureau of Standards, because the experiment needed conditions close to absolute zero so that a magnetic field could align the nuclear spins.

paras.lead: The result, in the small hours of 9 January
parts: By December 1956 the experiment already showed signs of an asymmetry. In the early hours of 9 January 1957 the result was confirmed: more electrons flew out in one direction; the mirror world was not the same. The paper was published on 15 February.
Leon Lederman and colleagues at Columbia also provided an independent check using meson decay. Parity nonconservation in the weak interaction was from then on a fact.

paras.lead: The prize was awarded that same year, 1957
parts: The Nobel Prize in Physics that year went to Chen-Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee. Wu’s name was not on the list. Nomination records later made public show that she received zero nominations in 1957 — the key paper appeared after the 31 January nomination deadline, so she did not meet the procedural conditions for sharing the prize that year.

According to the nomination archive now published on the Nobel Prize website through 1975, she received 26 nominations for the physics prize across 11 years between 1958 and 1975, including three from Tsung-Dao Lee; the prize was never later awarded for this experiment.

paras.lead: No prize, but still a place
parts: She was the first woman to receive tenure in Columbia’s physics department, was awarded the U.S. National Medal of Science in 1975, and in 1978 became the first recipient of the Wolf Prize in Physics. She died in New York on 16 February 1997, at the age of 84.

Later generations often called her “the Chinese Madame Curie.” The comparison spread her name, but it also makes it easy to reduce a first-rate experimental physicist to a symbol of “the woman scientist.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Chien-Shiung Wu｜View: Whether a symmetry is true must be settled by experiment.；Interest: Make a reliable measurement, and keep the rigor and priority of the experiment.；Worry: That the cryogenic apparatus would fail, or that someone else would publish first.；Basis: She chose the cobalt-60 design and worked with the National Bureau of Standards team.

Chen-Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee｜View: Parity conservation in the weak interaction was not beyond doubt.；Interest: That the theoretical prediction be confirmed.；Worry: Without experimental support, the challenge would not be accepted.；Basis: The October 1956 paper; the 1957 Nobel Prize was awarded for this theoretical work.

The Nobel Committee｜View: Under the statutes, the prize honors a discovery of the previous year, and the person must already have been nominated.；Interest: To uphold procedure and the definition of a “discovery.”；Worry: Waiting a year might mean losing prompt recognition of a major breakthrough.；Basis: The 1957 archive shows she had zero nominations that year; the committee awarded the prize to Yang and Lee.

Other experimental groups at the time｜View: The same prediction could be tested by different methods.；Interest: The scientific standing that comes with an independent confirmation.；Worry: Publishing later than Wu.；Basis: The meson experiment by Lederman and others produced evidence at almost the same time.

Later historians of science｜View: Procedure can explain 1957, but it cannot fully explain why the prize was never awarded later.；Interest: To understand how scientific honor is distributed.；Worry: Reducing a complicated process to a single story of discrimination — or, equally, denying any injustice at all.；Basis: The archive of 26 nominations is public (the website is currently open through 1975); analyses of the reasons still differ.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The theory was published first, and the prize was awarded unusually quickly, so the experimentalist was left outside the timetable.
Several groups confirmed the result at the same time, which sped recognition and also scattered the question of who should share the honor.
She received tenure and major awards, but she never received the prize the public notices most.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Scientific discoveries are often completed by theory and experiment together; the honors system often has room to recognize only one stretch of the work.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: How Yang and Lee described their discussions with Wu in the 1956 paper has been interpreted in ways that are not entirely consistent.
“Gender or ethnic discrimination was the main cause” is not written in the archive as a single conclusion, and this article does not settle the question.
Technical details such as the lowest temperature reached in the experiment differ slightly from one memoir to another.

pieces.title: Two needle tips rewrote the electrical age: eighty years of the transistor
pieces.hook: On 16 December 1947, at Bell Labs, Bardeen and Brattain pressed two extremely fine gold-foil tips into…
pieces.imageAlt: A replica of the first transistor
pieces.imageCredit: U.S. federal government employee · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 16 December 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed two extremely fine gold-foil tips into a germanium crystal and, for the first time, made a solid-state device amplify an electrical signal. Until then, radios and telephone exchanges had depended on vacuum tubes that were fragile, power-hungry, and ran hot.
An electronic world small enough to fit in a pocket began at those two needle tips.

On 23 December they demonstrated the point-contact transistor to the laboratory’s director. Bell Labs announced it publicly on 30 June 1948. William Shockley then proposed and realized the junction transistor, which was better suited to manufacturing; the three men shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work.
Relations after the invention were not happy: credit, patents, and temperament pulled the group taut.

paras.lead: From the laboratory onto the shelf
parts: Early transistors were expensive and unstable. In 1951 Western Electric began producing point-contact transistors at scale. In 1954 Texas Instruments made a silicon transistor, and the first transistor radios appeared the same year.

Electronic devices became, for the first time, truly lighter and more efficient. In 1958 and 1959, Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce each produced an integrated circuit, putting many transistors into a single piece of material. In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of components on a chip roughly doubled at a regular interval; the rule of thumb became known as Moore’s Law, and later set the rhythm of the whole industry.

In 1956 semiconductors were placed on China’s list of urgent scientific measures. That November, the Institute of Applied Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences produced China’s first germanium alloy-junction transistor. In 1958, China’s first semiconductor-device plant, Factory 109, was established; by 1960 the plant could already make more than a dozen types and more than 140,000 germanium transistors, used in computers and other equipment.
The starting point came nine years after Bell Labs, but the direction was already clear: without the transistor, there is no modern computing.

paras.lead: The workshop moves to the nanometer scale
parts: What followed is the story of Silicon Valley, wafer fabs, and lithography machines. Chip processes moved from micrometers into nanometers; design, fabrication, and packaging were split into a global division of labor. The control systems of phones, computers, cars, and power plants all rest, at the bottom, on the switching of vast numbers of transistors.

The industry also became extremely capital-intensive: an advanced plant often costs tens of billions of dollars, a few steps are highly concentrated, and technology and geopolitics have become tightly bound.

Faster, and more crowded】The transistor has not been replaced; it has only been made extremely small and extremely dense. The physical room left for Moore’s Law has narrowed, and people now use more complex packaging, new materials, and specialized chips to keep performance rising. Countries treat semiconductors as infrastructure, not merely as a business.
What those two needle tips opened in 1947 is a race that is still being raised, even now.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The inventors and the laboratory｜View: Replace the vacuum tube with a solid-state device.；Interest: Patents, scientific honor, and the reliability of the telephone system.；Worry: That the device would be unstable, or that credit would be divided unevenly.；Basis: The 1947 experiment succeeded; the three shared the 1956 Nobel, but relations inside the group were strained.

Manufacturers｜View: Whoever can produce at stable volume defines the next generation of products.；Interest: Profit and process barriers.；Worry: The investment is huge, and the next generation arrives before the last one has earned its cost back.；Basis: From Western Electric and Texas Instruments to later wafer fabs, manufacturing capability has been treated as the core.

Downstream electronics, auto, and telecom firms｜View: Smaller, more efficient, cheaper chips open new markets.；Interest: Product cycles.；Worry: Supply being stuck at a handful of plants.；Basis: The transistor radio, the computer, and the smartphone appeared in turn.

National governments｜View: Semiconductors are a matter of security and industrial sovereignty.；Interest: Autonomy in computing, communications, and defense.；Worry: Export controls and supply-chain breaks.；Basis: China listed them as an urgent measure in 1956; in recent years many countries have adopted chip-industry policies.

Scientists and engineers｜View: Even as physical limits close in, the next jump still has to be found.；Interest: Breakthroughs in new structures and new materials.；Worry: Costs rising faster than performance gains.；Basis: Advanced packaging and specialized chips have become the main ways of extending progress.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The laboratory wants a discovery; the factory wants yield. Their tempos differ, and neither can do without the other.
Globalization brought costs down, and also concentrated risk in a few plants and a few pieces of equipment.
Governments’ security concerns are rewriting a division of labor that firms and engineers had grown used to.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The transistor made the world smaller; to keep making it smaller looks less and less like a single invention, and more like a collective, money-burning campaign.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Early production figures come from company and museum sources, and the statistical definitions are not uniform.
Figures such as “Factory 109 produced 145,000 units in 1960” rest on plant histories from the Chinese Academy of Sciences system.
Estimates of the current global semiconductor market’s latest total differ by institution; this article does not adopt a single unchecked number.

pieces.title: A hot spell, and boot sales fell 20 percent: Dr. Martens’ half-year accounts
pieces.hook: Before the London market opened on 12 November, the British footwear brand Dr. Martens (the boots people usually call…
pieces.event: 2026-11-12 (London): first-half results released before the opening bell; the stock closed down 14.67% that day
pieces.imageAlt: A pair of brown Dr. Martens 1460 boots

parts: Before the London market opened on 12 November, the British footwear brand Dr. Martens (the boots people usually call Docs; London ticker DOCS) reported results for the 26 weeks to 27 September — the first half of fiscal 2027: revenue was £290.4 million, 9.8% below the £322 million of a year earlier, or 9.2% lower at constant currency. The share price closed down 14.67% that day, at 54.10 pence, the steepest fall in the FTSE 250.

On 1 April 1960, the first eight-eyelet 1460 boot came off the line in Northamptonshire, England; the model number is simply that date. The air-cushioned sole and yellow stitching first appealed to workers who wanted something that would last; later, musicians and a range of subcultures took the boots onto the street.
The brand now sells in more than 60 countries and employs about 3,600 people; some “Made in England” styles are still produced at the old factory in Northamptonshire.

First-half boot revenue fell 20%, and boots’ share of total revenue slipped from 49% to 44%. The company put it plainly in the release: the core boot category was hit by “unseasonably hot summer weather,” especially in Europe. Shoes rose 1%, and their share climbed to 41%; sandals rose 5%, to 11% of sales; bags and accessories were down 11%.
The company sold 4.2 million pairs, against 4.7 million a year earlier — a drop of about a tenth.

By market, U.K. revenue fell 21.3% at constant currency, the United States 5.1%; the German-speaking region and Japan were roughly flat (down 2.3% and 2.5% respectively). The “other direct markets” that include France, Italy, and Spain fell 12.9%, where consumer confidence was weak and the weather especially hot; South Korea and China were among the few bright spots. In the same period the company was also switching to a new website; after the launch, traffic and conversion fell as expected, and the company deliberately spent less on performance advertising.

paras.lead: Gross margin held; the loss still widened
parts: The gross margin held at 65.3%, and other operating costs fell 8.6% at constant currency, or about £13 million. But the drop in revenue was too large: the adjusted pretax loss widened from £9.4 million to £13.7 million. The reported pretax loss was £8.5 million, actually smaller than the £11 million of a year earlier.
Operating cash outflow was £33 million (against £9.1 million last year), in part because the company was stocking up for the year-end peak. The interim dividend was held at 0.85 pence a share.

paras.lead: Why the share price fell so hard
parts: First, the company gave no full-year figures: it said October had improved on a very weak September, but was still running at a year-on-year decline of more than ten percentage points, in line with the second quarter. The weeks of Black Friday, the run-up to Christmas, and the post-holiday markdowns were “critical to the full-year result,” and the range of outcomes for full-year revenue and profit was “wide.” The release also listed the analyst consensus: full-year revenue of £777 million and adjusted pretax profit of £65.7 million.

Second, the numbers were weaker than brokers had expected. According to Investing.com, Peel Hunt had forecast first-half revenue of £318 million and that day cut its rating by one notch from “buy.” Intraday the shares touched a 52-week low of 52.1 pence.

The figures for revenue, categories, volumes, and cash flow come from the company’s results release of 12 November; the closing price comes from Sharecast’s close that day. That “hot weather was the main cause” is the company’s own explanation. The especially deep fall in the U.K. also had to do with a weak market and the overhaul of the direct-to-consumer site; the release does not break out how much of the decline was weather.
The above is an account of a market reaction that has already happened, not a judgment on the shares.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Company management｜View: The brand is still strong; the problem is the weather and the short-term pain of a planned website overhaul.；Interest: Reduce reliance on boots, and push the new brand platform “With Bouncing Soles” and a new sandal range.；Worry: That the Black Friday and Christmas weeks will not sell, and the full-year result will land at the low end of the range.；Basis: The 12 November release: chief executive Ije Nwokorie called the first half “disappointing”; a new sandal range is due in spring/summer 2027, and new brand centers have opened in Paris, New York, and Munich.

Shareholders and brokers｜View: Giving no full-year guidance leaves the uncertainty with investors.；Interest: Predictable profits and dividends.；Worry: That the consensus pretax profit of £65.7 million will be missed.；Basis: The shares closed down 14.67% that day (Sharecast); Peel Hunt cut its rating (Investing.com).

Wholesale customers (department stores and shoe shops)｜View: Orders are recovering, but they will wait to see peak-season sell-through before restocking.；Interest: Goods that sell and do not sit in inventory.；Worry: That weather and weak consumer confidence will keep dragging on retail.；Basis: The release said wholesale, 46% of revenue, outperformed direct-to-consumer; the company has “good visibility” on the order book for the coming months.

Consumers｜View: In hot weather they do not want boots, and switch to shoes and sandals.；Interest: Comfort, durability, and a reasonable price.；Worry: The cost of living is high, and non-essential shoes can wait.；Basis: Shoes +1%, sandals +5%; the release noted especially weak consumer confidence in France, Italy, and Spain, and a sluggish U.K. market.

Banks and creditors｜View: The half-year end is normally the high point of the year’s debt.；Interest: Interest and principal paid on time.；Worry: A missed peak season, and tighter cash.；Basis: Net bank debt was £158.9 million, roughly in line with £154.3 million a year earlier; cash at period-end was £91.1 million (against £180.3 million at the start).

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The company wants to spread risk with sandals and shoes, but boots still account for more than 40% of revenue; one hot summer is enough to drag down a whole half year.
The website overhaul is for the long term, but it costs traffic in the short term; management and shareholders do not have the same patience for how long the pain can last.
Wholesale customers hold the order book, but whether they restock depends on whether consumers spend in the peak season.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The full-year accounts will rest largely on the ten or so weeks from November to early January; the company has offered a “wide range,” and the market wants a single number. That gap cannot, for now, be closed.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The company did not separately quantify how much of the sales movement was weather; “a hot summer was the main cause” is management’s account.
Peel Hunt’s forecast and rating change are cited from Investing.com; the original research note was not published.
The closing price of 54.10 pence and the 14.67% decline come from Sharecast’s close that day; intraday figures differ slightly from one report to another.

pieces.title: A governing party voted no, and the bill still passed: the night the Netherlands voted 76 to 74
pieces.short: The night the Netherlands voted 76 to…
pieces.hook: On the evening of 12 November, the Dutch House of Representatives (150 seats) passed, by 76 votes to 74,…
pieces.event: 2026-11-12 (The Hague): the House of Representatives voted on the 2027 tax plan; at the time of writing, the coalition’s future was still unsettled
pieces.imageAlt: The plenary hall of the Dutch House of Representatives at its temporary site
pieces.imageCredit: Jeroen van der Meyde / Dutch House of Representatives · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On the evening of 12 November, the Dutch House of Representatives (150 seats) passed the government’s Tax Plan 2027 by 76 votes to 74 — just over half. Strangely, one of the three governing parties, the People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD), voted against it; the votes that carried the government over the line came instead from several opposition parties.

The cabinet of Prime Minister Rob Jetten (D66) was sworn in on 23 February 2026, a coalition of D66, the VVD, and the Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA). Together the three parties hold only 66 seats, short of a majority: it is a minority government, and every bill has to find extra votes in parliament.

The tax plan decides how the government will raise money next year, and the three parties talked for weeks without agreeing. D66 and the CDA finally reached an amendment with the opposition left-wing party Pro and the pan-European progressive party Volt: shifting about €1 billion of the tax burden from wage-earners onto the wealthy.

Of that, nearly €900 million would be used to hold down a planned rise in the lowest income-tax bracket. Tax on savings and investment income would be split into two bands, 35.5% on annual returns up to €60,000 and 38.5% on the rest. The practice of parents making “paper gifts” to children in order to pay less gift and inheritance tax would also be tightened. The amendment passed with 79 votes.

The VVD held that the amendment violated the three parties’ coalition agreement, and had already said in advance that if the amendment passed it would vote against the tax plan as a whole. After the vote, the VVD’s parliamentary leader, Ruben Brekelmans, called the day “embarrassing,” and also said he would “not take a decision two minutes after the vote.”
The public broadcaster NOS pointed to the awkwardness: a tax plan rewritten from the left would have to be carried out by a finance minister who comes from the VVD.

paras.lead: How the last two votes were found
parts: Without the VVD, D66 and the CDA could only look left to reach 76. The Party for the Animals (PvdD) had still said the day before that it would vote no, then changed its mind before the vote, in exchange for a higher tax on private jets and the cancellation of a planned rise in train fares. The Denk party also joined at the last moment; what it received in return, NOS said, was not clear.

The final yes votes came from D66, the CDA, Pro, Volt, 50PLUS, the Christian Union, Denk, and the Party for the Animals. The right-wing Party for Freedom (PVV) immediately tabled a motion of no confidence in the cabinet, which was defeated by 34 votes to 116.

Before the vote, the cabinet wrote to parliament recommending that the amendment not be adopted. According to the Dutch news agency ANP, as reported by NL Times, the reasons were technical: the plan counted on €400 million from cracking down on tax avoidance — about 40% of the extra revenue — but most of that still had no concrete measures; and a new tax on investment returns of the wealthy might not come into force until 2029.

The tax plan still has to pass the Senate, where the three governing parties are likewise short of a majority. Jetten called it “a situation I have never encountered in all my years in The Hague,” though he did not use the word “crisis.” He said the three parties would have to “make a very serious fresh start,” and arranged to meet on the morning of 13 November with the two deputy prime ministers — VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz and the CDA’s Bart van den Brink.
At the time of writing (the early morning of 13 November, Beijing time), the VVD had not yet said whether it would leave the cabinet.

blocks.title: How a minority government gets a bill through
blocks.text: When the governing parties do not have a majority in parliament, they have to borrow votes from the opposition every time: talking to the left today, to the right tomorrow. The advantage is flexibility; the disadvantage is that once coalition partners each go looking for their own allies, you can get a night like this one, when your own side votes no and your opponents help you over the line. Jetten said he had also talked earlier with parties on the right, including JA21 and BBB, and that those talks had stalled on immigration and nitrogen policy, respectively.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Prime Minister Jetten and D66｜View: Better to “make a serious fresh start” than to let the cabinet fall.；Interest: Keep the government, and get next year’s tax cuts and budget in place.；Worry: That the VVD will walk out, making it even harder for a minority government to find votes.；Basis: NL Times, 11-12: he ruled out a cabinet without VVD ministers, and arranged to meet the two deputy prime ministers.

The VVD｜View: The amendment violated the coalition agreement and turned too far to the left.；Interest: Hold the line against tax increases, and hold onto its own voters.；Worry: That its own finance minister would have to carry out a tax plan rewritten from the left.；Basis: Brekelmans spoke against the plan and called the day “embarrassing”; party leader Yeşilgöz on 11 November called for a “fundamental reset” (NOS).

The CDA｜View: Find a majority in the center, get the budget through first, and avoid chaos.；Interest: Push the plan through and keep the centrist position.；Worry: Being caught between the VVD and the left, pleasing neither side.；Basis: After the vote, parliamentary leader Bontenbal said: “I hope this makes us stronger” (NOS).

The opposition left, Pro and Volt｜View: Make the wealthy pay a little more, and ease the burden on wage-earners.；Interest: Write a “millionaire’s tax” into the national budget.；Worry: The original plan was €1.5 billion; only about €1 billion remains, and another €400 million is still not nailed down.；Basis: Pro leader Klaver: “A center-left majority is taking responsibility for governing the country; that way chaos is avoided” (DutchNews).

Right-wing opposition parties (PVV, JA21, BBB, and others)｜View: This cabinet should go.；Interest: Use the turmoil to press for early elections or a larger voice.；Worry: That a center-left majority will take shape and leave them outside.；Basis: The PVV’s no-confidence motion won only 34 votes; Jetten said talks with JA21 and BBB had stalled on immigration and nitrogen policy, respectively.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: D66 and the CDA used votes from the left to get the plan through, at the price of the VVD’s trust; the VVD wants to stay in government, but does not want to underwrite someone else’s tax reform.
The one or two votes in the hands of small parties such as the Party for the Animals and Denk became, in a 76-to-74 contest, bargaining chips for a private-jet tax and train fares.
The cabinet itself recommended rejecting the amendment, yet a governing party voted for it — the government and the parliamentary groups were not speaking with one voice.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The plan has passed the House, but the government may yet come apart over it: whether the VVD stays or goes, and whether the Senate can also find the votes, are two gates that still have no answer.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: How each party voted, and the amendment’s vote totals, come from reporting by NOS, DutchNews, NRC, and other outlets; the official House record had not been checked item by item at the time of writing.

When the €400 million of tax-avoidance revenue will actually arrive is not described consistently: NL Times said the new tax might not start until 2029, while DutchNews wrote that it would be sought from 2028.
What the Denk party received in return for supporting the plan has not been made public.
